4. Her former husband, which sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before the Lord: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin, which the Lord thy God giveth thee. for an inheritance.
4. Non poterit maritus ejus prior, quia eam a se demisit, reverti, et ducere eam sibi uxorem, posteaquam polluta est: quia abominatio est coram facie Jehovae: et non inquinabis peccato terram quam Jehova Deus tuus tradet tibi in haereditatem.
entries.1029398449b0bf082439154fd02fc7305d5b1bd3: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.22.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.22.22" sID="gen15093" type="section"/><p/> <div sID="gen15094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.22.22">Deuteronomy 22:22</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">If</hi> <hi type="italic">a</hi> <hi type="italic">man</hi> <hi type="italic">be</hi> <hi type="italic">found</hi> <hi type="italic">lying</hi> <hi type="italic">with</hi>. A Political Supplement, whereby it appears how greatly God abominates adultery, since He denounces capital punishment against it. And assuredly, since marriage is a covenant consecrated by God, its profanation is in no wise tolerable; and conjugal faith should be held too sacred to be violated with impunity, whilst it is an act of horrible perfidiousness to snatch from a man’s bosom the wife who is as his very life, or at any rate half of himself. Wherefore, also, the Prophet ignominiously compares adulterers to neighing horses, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.5.8">Jeremiah 5:8</reference>;) for where such lasciviousness prevails, men degenerate, as it were, into beasts. Another reason is, however, here referred to; for, if a man had broken faith with his wife by having connection with a harlot, it was not a capital offense; but if any man, though a bachelor, had committed adultery with the wife of another, (he was to die, <note n="68"> <div sID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> Added from <hi type="italic">Fr</hi>.<div eID="gen15095" type="x-p"/> </note> ) because both the husband is grossly injured, and the dishonor descends to the offspring, and all adulterine race is substituted in place of the legitimate one, whilst the inheritance is transferred to strangers, and thus bastards unlawfully possess themselves of the family name. This cause impelled the Gentiles, even before the Law, to punish adultery with severity, as clearly appears from the history of Judah and Tamar. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Gen.38.14">Genesis 38:14</reference>.) Nay, by the universal law of the Gentiles, the punishment of death was always awarded to adultery; wherefore it is all the baser and more shameful in Christians not to imitate at least the heathen. Adultery is punished no less severely by the Julian law <note n="69"> <div sID="gen15096" type="x-p"/> See Plin., <reference osisRef="">Ep. 6:13</reference>.<div eID="gen15096" type="x-p"/> </note> than by that of God; whilst those who boast themselves of the Christian name are so tender and remiss, that they visit this execrable offense with a very light reproof. And lest they should abrogate God’s law without a pretext, they allege the example of Christ, who dismissed the woman taken in adultery, whereas she ought to have been stoned; just as He withdrew Himself into a mountain that He might not be made a king by the multitude. (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.8.11">John 8:11</reference>, and 6:15.) For if we consider what the office was which the Father delegated to His only-begotten Son, we shall not be surprised that He was content with the limits of His vocation, and did not discharge the duties of a Judge. But those who have been invested with the sword for the correction of crime, have absurdly imitated His example, and thus their relaxation of the penalty has flowed from gross ignorance.<div eID="gen15094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15097" type="x-p"/>Although the disloyalty of husband and wife are not punished alike by human tribunals, still, since they are under mutual obligation to each other, God will take vengeance on them both; and hence the declaration of Paul takes effect before the judgment-seat of God, Let not married persons defraud one another; for the wife hath not power of her own body, nor the husband of his. (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.7.4 Bible:1Cor.7.5">1 Corinthians 7:4, 5</reference>.)<div eID="gen15097" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.22.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen15093" osisID="Deut.22.22" type="section"/>

23. If a damsel that is a virgin be betrothed. The severity of the punishment is now extended further, and a betrothed woman is counted as a wife; and this for a very good reason, because she has plighted her troth, and it is a token of abandoned incontinency for the mind of a woman to be so alienated from the man to whom she is betrothed, as to prostitute her virginity to another’s embraces. But since one who has been ravished is not criminal, a woman is absolved if she be forced in a field, because it is probable that she yielded unwillingly, inasmuch as she was far from assistance. Although, however, the terms are accommodated to the comprehension of a rude people, it was the intention of God to distinguish force from consent. Thus if a girl had been forced in a retired part of a building, from whence her cries could not be heard, God would undoubtedly have her acquitted, provided she could prove her innocence by satisfactory testimony and conjecture.

30. A man shall not take his father’s wife. Since Moses does not here refer to any other kinds of incest, but speaks only of that with a step-mother, it is probable that, what he had more fully set forth before he here briefly recalled to the minds of the Israelites under a single head. At any rate, the prohibition of one offense does not open the gate to other abominations. The expression which he adds, “nor discover his father’s skirt,” is as much as to say, that the father is exposed to shame when the step-son has; no regard to decency, and goes in to his step-mother. Perhaps he alludes to the sin of Ham, who betrayed his ungodliness by exposing the shame of his father. (Genesis 9:22.)

                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And they shall amerce him in an hundred <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver, and give <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> unto the father of the damsel <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Because this was a reproach to his family, and to himself, because such a miscarriage of his Daughters would have been ascribed to his evil education.</ns0:note> because he hath brought up an evil name upon a virgin of Israel: and she shall be his wife, he may not put her away all his dayes <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Which seems to have been his design in this false accusation, and therefore that liberty of a divorce which is permitted to others, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24. 1. shall be denied to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 But if this thing be true, <ns0:hi>and the tokens of</ns0:hi> virginity be not found for the damsel:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 Then they shall bring out the damsel to the door of her fathers house, and the men of her city shall stone her with stones, that she die <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>Qu.</ns0:hi> Why should she die when her crime was onely Fornica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion, which was not punished in a woman with death, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 16, 17? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> Because there was not onely Fornication in this case, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> but this was accompanyed with deep dissimulation and injury to her Husband in the false profession of Virginity, and it might be presumed that she committed this folly after she was betrothed to him, and therefore so obstinately denyed it, as knowing the danger of it in that case; Or God ordered it thus for the honour and custody of the matrimonial bed from all defilement, that she, who being defiled before she was married or betrothed, and therefore not punishable by death, yet if she should presume to carry her defilement into the married estate with a pretence of Virginity, she should then be put to death.</ns0:note>, because she hath wrought folly in Israel, to play the whore in her fathers house: so <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 13. 5.</ns0:note> shalt thou put evil away from among you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 20. 10.</ns0:note> If a man be found lying with a woman marryed <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">If he be convicted of this fault, though not taken in the very act.</ns0:note> to an husband, then they shall both of them die: <ns0:hi>both</ns0:hi> the man that lay with the wo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />man, and the woman: so shalt thou put away evil from Israel.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 If a damsel <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> a virgin be betrothed un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />to an husband <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">For by this betrothing she had actually engaged her self to another man, and was in some sort his Wife, and therefore is sometimes so called, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 29. 21. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 1. 20.</ns0:note>, and a man find her in the city, and lie with her:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Then ye shall bring them both out unto the gate of that city, and ye shall stone them with stones, that they die: the damsel because she cri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed not <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">And therefore is justly presumed to have consented to it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>being</ns0:hi> in the city: and the man because he hath humbled his neighbors wife: so thou shalt put away evil from among you.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 But if a man find a betrothed damsel in the field, and the man <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> force her <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which was to be examined and determined by the consi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />deration of all the circumstances.</ns0:note>, and lie with her: then the man onely that lay with her shall die.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 But unto the damsel thou shalt do nothing, <ns0:hi>there is</ns0:hi> in the damsel no sin <ns0:hi>worthy</ns0:hi> of death: for as when a man riseth against his neighbour and slayeth him, even so <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this matter <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Not an act of choice, but of force and constraint.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 For he found her in the field, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> the betro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thed damsel cried <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Which is in that case to be presumed, charity obliging us to believe the best till the contrary be manifest.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> none to save her.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 22. 16.</ns0:note> If a man <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) An unmarried man, as appears, 1. From his obli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gation to marry the person he abused, which it is not probable would have been imposed upon him. 2. Because if the man had been married, this had been adultery, and so had been pu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nished with death.</ns0:note> find a damsel <ns0:hi>that is</ns0:hi> a virgin, which is not betrothed, and lay hold on her <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Which notes some kind of force or ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tifice whereby she was overpowred, whereas <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 16. she was enticed, which implies consent, and therefore the man doth here receive a greater punishment, because he used hostile violence towards her, which was the greater sin.</ns0:note>, and lie with her, and they be found:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Then the man that lay with her shall give unto the damsels father fifty <ns0:hi>shekels</ns0:hi> of silver <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Besides the dowry, as <ns0:hi>Philo</ns0:hi> the Learned <ns0:hi>Iew</ns0:hi> notes, which is here omitted, because that was common and custo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mary, and because it might easily be gathered out of <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 16. it being sufficient here to mention what was peculiar to this case.</ns0:note>, and she shall be his wife <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, if her Father consent to it, which is to be supposed out of <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 16. it being not likely that the Father should lose his paternal right of disposing his Child when she was in some sort forced, rather than when she was inticed.</ns0:note>, because he hath hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bled her: he may not put her away all his dayes <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Which others were suffered to do, <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 24. 1. and he who inticed the maid, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22. 16. was not prohibi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
